questions.question: Define a structure and explain, with examples, why a heap of bricks is not one while a paper cup is.
questions.expected_answer: A structure is an arrangement of parts joined so that it holds its shape and carries a load, such as its own weight, what it carries, or wind and water pressing on it. A heap of bricks has no arrangement and no part helps carry another, so it is not a structure. A paper cup, although small and light, has a shape it keeps and contains and supports a load of liquid, so it is a structure; size is not what matters.

questions.question: Name the four purposes of structures, give one example of each from a street in a South African town, and describe one structure that serves more than one purpose.
questions.expected_answer: Contain: a water tank holding water. Protect: a house keeping a family dry and safe. Support: a tank stand or a cell phone mast holding antennas high. Span: a footbridge crossing a stormwater canal. A house serves more than one purpose: it protects its occupants and contains their belongings, while its roof spans the rooms and its walls support the roof.

questions.question: Explain the difference between natural and man-made structures and give two examples of design ideas that people have borrowed from natural structures.
questions.expected_answer: Natural structures are made by nature without human help, such as trees, nests, webs, shells and termite mounds; man-made structures are designed and built by people, such as houses, bridges, towers and chairs, and the classification depends on who made it, not on the material. Borrowed ideas include hollow reed stems inspiring stiff light tubes for masts; the honeycomb's hexagons stiffening panels and cardboard; the egg shell dome inspiring stadium roofs; and termite mound air channels inspiring a naturally cooled shopping centre in Harare.
